correctness.rationale: For A=[[a,c],[c,b]] SPD set rho=|c|/sqrt(ab), q=sqrt((a−b)^2+4c²)/(a+b). Direct exact algebra gives q²−rho²=(a−b)²(ab−c²)/(ab(a+b)²)≥0, and the increasing function (1+t)/(1−t) proves κ(J(A))≤κ(A), with equality precisely at a=b. In n=3 the rank-one Aκ has eigenvalues (1,1,κ); use interchange symmetry of coordinates 2 and 3 to diagonalize J in antisymmetric and two-dimensional symmetric sectors. The least eigenvalue is 9/(4κ+5), and ratio λmax/λmin equals [2κ+1+2(κ−1)sqrt((κ+2)/(κ+8))]/3. Its excess above κ is (κ−1)(2sqrt((κ+2)/(κ+8))−1)/3>0 for all κ>1; large-κ ratio→4/3. Independently checked symbolic rank-one identities with Sympy and at κ=10 exact equilibrated eigenvalues (1/5,(7±2√6)/5), giving κ(J)=7+2√6>10. The original proof, not finite evaluations, establishes all κ.

value.rationale: A useful boundary for widely used diagonal preconditioning: universal harmlessness through dimension two versus a quantified failure already in three dimensions, for each given original condition number. The explicit rank-one family and limiting 4/3 factor clarify a practical numerical misconception without claiming globally worst possible inflation.

final_claim: For real 1×1 and 2×2 SPD matrices, symmetric Jacobi diagonal equilibration never raises κ₂, but dimension 3 permits strict worsening for every prescribed κ>1 via Aκ=I+((κ−1)/9)(1,−2,−2)(1,−2,−2)^T; the Jacobi κ₂ is explicit and its ratio tends to 4/3.
